newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE-Cigar smoking catches on in Philippines.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Cigar smoking catches on in Philippines.

text.p: It was a New Year's Eve party at one of Manila's most elegant hotels. Women in evening gowns and men in dinner jackets thronged dinner tables and the dance floor as a band played from the balcony.

After the clock struck midnight, as champagne was sipped and the strains of Auld Lang Syne died away, pungent smoke wafted across table after table as many of the men, and some of the women, lit up cigars.
It's a trend that is becoming increasingly popular among Filipinos.
Cigar smoking is beginning to cut across age barriers, professions and in some cases gender, says Katrina Panlilio, who owns the Tabac cigar shop.
"A lot of people now are trying it for status but there are people who are switching from smoking cigarettes," she says, in between puffs from a cheroot. "Suddenly, it has become popular."
"Now it's not evil to smoke a cigar," said Gabriel Ripoll, the managing director of cigar manufacturer Tabaqueria de Filipinas Inc.
"Some time ago, not too long ago, if you were a cigar-smoker, you were considered a gangster or a con man. Now, it's seen in its proper perspective."
WORLD-CLASS BUSINESS
Cigars are big business in the Philippines, the only Asian country to manufacture world-class cigars.
Ripoll says he produces about three million cigars per year and cannot keep up with demand.

The two-storeyed house where his factory is located is piled high with bales of tobacco leaf, mahogany cigar boxes and humidors. Employees work feverishly at tables rolling cigar leaf in wrappers, cutting, pressing and finally labelling and sheathing them in cellophane.
Others carve names on polished cigar boxes, manufactured by the company at a separate plant, and affix humidity gauges and rum-soaked sponges into humidors.
"We intend to increase our production by getting into a bigger building and training more people," Ripoll said. "Hopefully by August this year, we would be about more than double our capacity now."
He said more than three quarters of the company's output is aimed at overseas markets.

Originally, Philippine cigar tobacco came from seeds in Cuba, where the world's best cigars are manufactured. But now, because of the different climate and soil, local cigars have evolved a unique taste.
"It would be difficult to compete or to say that ours would be the same as the Cubans," said Ripoll. "Cuban cigars have their own mystique...although we come up with pretty good quality."
PRESIDENTIAL APPROVAL
One of the biggest promoters of Philippine cigars is President Fidel Ramos. He used to smoke, but now chews on an unlit corona several times a day.
He has in the past presented a box of Philippine cigars to another aficionado, who shares his first name -- President Fidel Castro of Cuba.
Brett Tolhurst, general manager of La Flor dela Isabela, one of the country's best known manufacturers, said his company supplies Ramos with a special brand of cigars not sold to anyone else.
"It's very secret, just for the president," he says. Asked if Ramos was charged for the deliveries, Tolhurst said: "He's a very good promoter of our products...we have a special arrangement."
The cigar business has a bright future in the Philippines, those in the industry said.

"The whole industry is becoming more of a lifestyle industry now," said Tolhurst. "You can see that with everything -- cigars good coffee, good wine. Those types of industries are really prospering and it is a boutique lifestyle."

Panlilio of Tabac holds a Friday evening get-together in her shop, serving a rum-based cocktail free of charge to customers to promote cigar smoking. She's also planning cigar dinners for women and regularly hosts an annual black-tie reception where rare cigars are auctioned.
STILL A HEALTH RISK
Although cigars are a health risk, smokers say they are less dangerous than cigarettes because the smoke is not supposed to be inhaled.

"With cigars you really savour the taste of the smoke itself, you don't inhale it," said Macy Tirador, a doctor who visits Panlilio's shop. "There are risks, but you know, life is too short. I just like smoking."
